The commentators cannot agree on when this was written, and most of them say so. Clarke relays the general view that it belongs to David's persecution by Saul, some placing it at the resolution to seek out Achish of Gath, and notes that the Greek Church has long used it at nightfall, adding candidly that several passages are very obscure. He also protests, against a common charge, that David's frequent opening complaints are nothing like habitual peevishness: troubles were frequent, help was always sought in the same quarter, and the devotion was never formal. Calvin cites the widely held opinion that it commemorates the cave of En-gedi, where David spared his persecutor and cut off only a skirt of his robe, and thinks the sixth verse points that way; yet he will venture nothing definite, allowing merely that he would not disapprove such a conjecture. Delitzsch situates it differently, tracing how closely these four neighbouring psalms are interwoven, and insists that a right grasp of the whole depends on identifying the circumstances, which the title by itself never settles.

On the prayer itself the readings converge and then diverge again. Spurgeon detects a last resort: the petition is painful, feeble, worthy of no better name than a cry, yet directed to Jehovah, and that ennobles it. Henry finds earnestness and fixity, remarking that pleaders may expect an audience, not for loudness but for liveliness. Augustine will not confine the utterance to one man: it belongs, he argues, chiefly to the Body, since when the Head knelt his sweat fell in great drops of blood, an image he applies to martyrdom throughout the Church; and he cautions that such crying cannot cease while tribulation lasts.

The incense and the evening sacrifice divide them on a point of fact. Henry supposes it offered in place of the altar rites David was banished from, and finds in the choice of dusk rather than dawn a pointer to Christ, who at the world's close offered himself. Clarke presses the Hebrew: the noun here is not the customary term for a slaughtered victim but the one naming an unbloody meal-gift, so no immolation is meant at all; barred from obeying the letter of the law far from the sanctuary, David serves in the spirit, and his raised hands substitute for that dusk oblation. Ellicott renders the opening verb as be erected and catches in it a column of smoke climbing steadily upward, adding that raised hands, given the parallelism, are plainly a figure for entreaty and no technical name for an offering. He notes too that some would refer the incense to the morning rite, so that the whole line asks that supplication rise as regularly as dawn and dusk observance, but judges this unnecessary, since the hour of composition seems itself to have been nightfall. Gill treats the frankincense as devotion made fragrant through Christ's mediation.

What follows they treat as a plea for the grace of silence. Delitzsch observes that a betrayed monarch's position demanded caution in speech, and that awareness of having offended God, whatever his innocence toward the rebels, blocked any outspoken self-defence. Spurgeon puts it warmly: lips lately employed in worship would be a pity to see defiled, and though we are ennobled by portering for God, he condescends to porter for us. Gill supposes the fear was of some rash utterance against Saul, the Lord's anointed, and on the following clause denies flatly that heaven ever bends anyone toward sin, construing the request as asking not to be abandoned to one's own corruption. Wesley would extend that guard beyond wicked talk to every evil stirring within, glossing the dainties as gains got by wickedness, whereas Ellicott suspects the noun means allurements, and points to the casuistries by which laxer Jews excused attending heathen banquets.
5:
The fifth verse is where the psalm turns hard, and every commentator says so. Ellicott opens by observing that the difficulties thicken here; Clarke calls the verse extremely difficult in the original; Delitzsch, having called the psalm comparatively easy to this point, says it now becomes difficult, yet not hopelessly so. The plain reading is Henry's: David asks to be told his faults, holds that reproof from the righteous is a kindness, and takes the oil for a healing application rather than an injury, since it is sin that has broken his head and the reproof is the ointment for the bruise. Gill and Wesley read it the same way, Wesley glossing the breaking as not hurting but healing and greatly refreshing.

The alternative depends on a different text. Clarke, following the Syriac, Vulgate, Greek, Ethiopic and Arabic, renders it so that the righteous man's chastisement is welcomed but the oil of the wicked is refused, and takes that oil for smooth flattering speech: David would rather suffer the cutting reproof of the righteous than the oily talk of the flatterer. Ellicott sets out both possibilities honestly. He notes the verb for smite is the one used of Jael's hammer strokes and that the word for reprove is probably judicial, admits the greatest obscurity attaches to the word rendered break, and says the older versions read anoint from a different text, which would remove the difficulty and yield an excellent parallelism. His paraphrase is that rather than join the wicked mirth of a profane banquet the poet would accept continued rebuke from one of the godly. Delitzsch keeps the received accents and refuses the rendering that makes the smiting conditional, since that would leave the subject twice unexpressed.

The sixth and seventh verses are harder still. Gill offers three constructions of the judges cast down by the rock, as prophecy of Gilboa, as Saul being let go free when David spared him, or as an imprecation. Clarke asks whether the rock is a fortress and its hands the garrison, tries the reading that the judges were dismissed in the rocky places and heard David's sweet words at En-gedi, then wonders whether the scattered bones are the priests massacred at Nob, in which case the phrase means at the command of Saul rather than at the grave's mouth, and finally admits that he could contend for his own conjectures but that they are all too vague. Ellicott hears irony instead: when the ungodly party's power is broken they will indeed hear the poet's words, and find how dainty they are, a song of triumph rather than a banquet song. He also prefers the plough to the woodcutter for the figure of the seventh verse, and reports the variant their bones, easier but for that reason to be rejected. Spurgeon keeps the received text and makes the bones the state of the godly cause under Saul, with no vitality, cohesion or headship left, split up and split for the fire.

The close is agreed. Henry has David casting himself on God when the case is otherwise past redress, and reads the last petition as justice and mercy together, the enemies falling into the net they meant for him. Gill takes the eyes lifted as body and mind at once, and identifies the snare with the wife given to trap David or with the Ziphites. Delitzsch notes how the psalm dies away in strains easy to understand and in keeping with the situation, and points out that the snare is pictured with hands, as though it seized. Ellicott makes the same idiom the clutches of the snare, and Clarke turns the last verse into a proverb: those who lay snares for others fall into them, and he has known families shot by the spring guns they set for thieves.
